theme: Give thanks to the LORD; he gathered the exiles
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 107:1-22. You read this passage on Day 442 as a song of rescue for those in every kind of trouble. Read it now as the psalm of the ones who have actually come home. Let the opening lines be the first words they said.
settingTheScene: Psalm 107 opens the last book of the Psalter with the words, “Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he has redeemed from trouble and gathered in from the lands.” That is the exact situation of Ezra’s generation. They were gathered from the east, the north, the south, and the west. On Day 442 you read this as the cry of those still waiting. Today, read it as the thanks of those who have returned and are rebuilding.
observation: “Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!” (v. 1).
“Let the redeemed of the LORD say so” (v. 2).
“Gathered in from the lands, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the south” (v. 3).
“He led them by a straight way till they reached a city to dwell in” (v. 7).
“Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of men!” (v. 8).
“For he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things” (v. 9).
“He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and burst their bonds apart” (v. 14).
“And let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving, and tell of his deeds in songs of joy!” (v. 22).
interpretation:
This is the testimony of the redeemed. The psalm does not tell them to wait until the story is complete. It tells them to say so. A redeemed person has something to say, and the first thing is thanks.

The first story is of wanderers in the desert, hungry and thirsty, who found no city to live in. Think of the caravan from Babylon, traveling over 800 miles to a city that lay in ruins. God “led them by a straight way till they reached a city to dwell in.” Their journey was real, and so was God’s guidance.

The second story is of prisoners in darkness. This is what the exile was. They were captives for rebelling against the words of God. And yet, when they cried out, “he burst their bonds apart.” The third is the sick, who were “fools through their sinful ways.” God’s word healed them.

What is the common thread? Each group was in trouble, each cried out, and each was rescued. Each time the response is the same: “Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works.” The psalm names what the right response is, thanks and sacrifice and songs of joy.

In the setting of the return, thanksgiving was also practical. The altar had been built, and sacrifices of thanksgiving were being offered. Telling of God’s deeds was part of the rebuilding. Remembering and recounting is what keeps the people alive. In the unit’s larger story, Chronicles will do the same on a larger scale, telling the whole history so that the community remembers who they are.
connection: Colossians 1:13-14 says God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son.” Luke 4:18-19: the Spirit anoints him to proclaim liberty to the captives. Ephesians 2:13 says that those who were far off have been brought near. Hebrews 13:15 invites us to offer a sacrifice of praise. 1 Peter 2:9: “that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.”
application:
Say it out loud: tell one person today what God has redeemed you from.

Write a short thank-you list in the pattern of the psalm: from what you were rescued, how you cried out, and how God answered.

Offer a “sacrifice of thanksgiving” this week, through a gift, a word of praise, or a service.
prayerPrompts: Give thanks to God for gathering you from a far place.
Let your own story say, “The LORD is good,” in your own words.
Thank him that his steadfast love endures forever.
